summary: Measured for FS-GG/.github#5182 (PR #5186). Over 2026-10-25..2026-11-01T12Z a .github PR head push started a mean 34-37 pull_request runs, plus about 2 pull_request_target runs. Each body edit, such as a routine-marker rebind, restarted about 4 more pull_request runs and the pull_request_target pair. In a 12-hour job sample (2,006 runs, 2,809 runner jobs), job queue wait (job created_at to started_at) had a p50 of 96 s and a p90 of 437 s. Workflows whose median job work was under 30 s produced 65.5 % of job starts but only 16.7 % of runner-minutes. Eight unfiltered, non-required gates (engine-flag-narrative, pipefail-assertions, signature-coverage, signature-doc-siting, prose-citations, telemetry-git-safety, v1-writer-census-advisory, wizard-graph-seal) each did a median 9-28 s of work after 80-130 s in the queue. Method lessons: (1) a run's run_started_at minus created_at was 0 for every run, so it is not a queue measure; use job timestamps. (2) Merging tiny workflows into one multi-job workflow cuts runs but not the runner slots that hosted concurrency limits; merging their steps into one job, with !cancelled() on every step, cuts both. (3) Path filters were not the lever for these gates, because each one states a whole-tree subject (see #930). (4) A static replay of real PR file sets against the workflow triggers gives a before/after that does not depend on load. On that replay the fold measured 38.2 to 31.2 workflows and 58.7 to 47.7 jobs per push. The queue effect after the change is unmeasured until later PRs report it (#5182 continues).
title: Tiny always-run PR gates cost runner slots, not work; measure queue from job timestamps
